restatement.intent: Run each unit of agent work as an isolated, non-interactive job whose prompt, tools and output contract are explicit and saved, so results can be compared, retried and audited.
restatement.problem: An agent run that inherits the operator's environment, stays conversational and answers in free text cannot be reproduced, compared across variants, or audited.
restatement.solution: Give each run its own directory and a run spec. Assemble and save a versioned prompt, and mount only least-privilege tools with read-only inputs and a fresh workspace. Invoke the agent non-interactively with ambient configuration off, and require one fenced JSON answer extracted with a fixed repair ladder. Batch variants in parallel under tags, skip valid answers, and retain events and transcripts.

quiz.answer: `--no-builtin-tools`, `--no-context-files`, `--no-skills` and `--no-prompt-templates`: they keep out the default built-in toolset, operator/project context files, skills, and prompt templates respectively. Tools then come only from a per-run MCP configuration.

quiz.answer: So parallel runs never share a writable directory, cache or answer file; each run gets isolated scratch space, and a builder run gets its own subdirectory containing only its inputs.

The dust project wrote the recipe three times with the same extraction code pasted into each script. The chapter recommends one runner driven by a run spec, with prompt parts and tool mounts as data, to remove the copies and their drift.

transfer.why: Thousands of findings are repeated, comparable units with a checkable verdict and reason; read-only code mounts and per-run isolation support parallel scoring, retries and later audit.

participants.Run spec: One finding at a pinned repository revision, model, thinking/decoding settings, prompt version and variant tag.
participants.Run directory: `runs/<tag>/<safe-run-id>/` holding the assembled prompt, tool config, workspace, event stream, transcript and answer.
participants.Prompt assembler: Role as security reviewer, triage criteria, required steps, known false-positive patterns, blind finding id and code pointers, output contract, and reference rules.
participants.Tool mount: Read-only checkout at the fixed commit, read-only code/search helpers, and a fresh empty workspace; no labels, prior triage decisions, or tests that reveal the intended verdict.
participants.Agent invocation: Non-interactive, with built-ins, context files, skills and templates off; only the mounted read/search tools exist.
participants.Extractor: Last fenced JSON object with `{finding_id, verdict: real|false_positive, reason, evidence}`, repaired through the fixed ladder and schema-validated.
participants.Batch runner: Runs findings in parallel, keeps variants apart by tag, skips only valid answers, retries failures, and preserves failure attempts.

transfer.sketch:
spec = RunSpec(finding.id, repo@commit, model, thinking, decoding, promptVersion, tag: 'triage-v1')

run(spec) → Answer | Failure
  dir = fresh(runsRoot / spec.tag / safe(spec.item.id))
  write(dir / 'prompt.md', assemble(spec.promptVersion, spec.item))
  write(dir / 'tools.json', mount(read: [checkout(spec.item.repo, spec.item.commit), helpersDir],
                                  write: dir / 'ws'))
  events = agent(cwd: dir, prompt: read(dir / 'prompt.md'), model: spec.model,
                 thinking: spec.thinking, decoding: spec.decoding,
                 builtinTools: none, contextFiles: none, skills: none, templates: none,
                 nonInteractive: true)
  write(dir / 'events.jsonl', events)
  exportTranscript(events, dir / 'transcript.html')
  return extract(events)

assemble(version, item) = join([role, criteria, steps, known_fp, describeBlind(item),
                                 contract, references])

batch(specs, workers: 8)
  todo = [s for s in specs if not validAnswer(s)]
  parallelMap(todo, s → finish(s, withTimeout(run(s), 15 min)), workers: 8)
key_notes: #1: switch off built-ins, context files, skills and templates, then mount only the triage tools; a read-only checkout still exposes credentials and network unless the run is in a container or empty environment.
#3: never mount the truth. Suppression comments, issue text, prior triage notes or tests naming the bug can leak the verdict; use blind ids and keep labels outside every mount.
#4: require one fenced JSON object with a literal schema example, validate the allowed verdict values, and log every repair.
#6 and #7: separate tag directories and per-run workspaces are essential for 5,000 parallel findings; otherwise runs collide and retries are ambiguous.
#8 and #11: state the code/evidence budget in the prompt and bound every run; a hung checkout or provider must not stall the batch.
#2: save the assembled prompt with each run; a surprising verdict is only diagnosable from the exact instructions and evidence the agent saw.
transfer.risk: The most likely error is mounting the whole repository, including issue text, suppression history or prior triage notes, which leaks the answer. A second risk is that one-finding isolation removes cross-file context needed for a fair verdict.

transfer.why: This is an open-ended, human-in-the-loop design conversation with no fixed work item, output contract or stable correctness criterion. Sealing each turn would remove the continuity and tacit context that make the collaboration useful.
key_notes: The chapter's first do-not-use bullet applies directly: sealing removes the conversation that makes the work possible.
There is no stable run spec or comparable variant; each draft depends on the designer's previous reactions and the shared thread.
A sealed run could be used after the conversation to evaluate finished landing-page candidates against a rubric, but that is downstream evaluation, not the brainstorming session.
transfer.risk: Forcing the pattern produces disconnected one-shot drafts and comparisons that measure prompt differences rather than design quality.

review_notes.note: The chapter calls the run a pure function and says nothing from the operator's environment survives, but note 1 admits environment variables, home-directory credentials and network access do survive, and Consequences admits routed model versions change. The function also depends on model, decoding and provider version, not just prompt and tools.
review_notes.suggestion: Define 'sealed' as closing the agent's configuration channels. Require a container, empty environment and network policy for the stronger claim, and call the result reproducible from recorded inputs rather than pure.

review_notes.note: RunSpec contains `decoding`, but `run()` never passes it to `agent()`, and the Structure table omits decoding. As written, temperature, maxTokens and seed are not part of the invocation.
review_notes.suggestion: Pass `decoding: spec.decoding` and record the provider-reported model version, agent version and tool-config hash alongside the spec.

review_notes.note: The skip test uses `hash(spec)`, but the spec carries labels such as `promptVersion`, not the contents of the assembled prompt or tool mount. Editing a prompt part behind the same version label, or changing the tool config, leaves the hash unchanged. Two concurrent batches can also both pass the exists check.
review_notes.suggestion: Content-address the spec with hashes of the assembled prompt, tool config, agent/provider version and decoding. Claim the answer path with a lock or create-exclusive run record.

review_notes.note: `fresh(run dir)` on a retry wipes the failed attempt's events and transcript, so the audit trail is lost exactly when a failure is being investigated.
review_notes.suggestion: Keep attempt subdirectories or append-only attempt records and point the answer at the successful attempt; do not delete failed evidence.

review_notes.note: The repair ladder names `rawNewlines`, `droppedKey`, `bareIdColon`, `innerQuotes` and `mismatchedClosers` but never defines them or gives examples. Order matters, and a repair can turn a wrong answer into a parseable one. The pseudocode also has no Failure branch when `validate(obj, schema)` rejects the object.
review_notes.suggestion: Show before/after examples, fix the order, validate after every repair, log both raw and repaired blocks, and fail closed on ambiguity.

review_notes.note: The run path `runsRoot / tag / item.id` assumes item ids are unique and path-safe. Two repositories can reuse a finding id, and an id containing separators can escape the directory; joins on item ids across repositories become ambiguous.
review_notes.suggestion: Use an opaque, sanitized run id and store a canonical work-item key such as repository, revision and finding id. Reject unsafe path components.

review_notes.note: Counting every failed run as a wrong answer conflates task accuracy with infrastructure reliability. A variant with more provider timeouts will look less accurate even if its failure rate is also reported.
review_notes.suggestion: Report accuracy on valid completed runs and reliability separately, use paired item comparisons and confidence intervals, and do not let infrastructure failures silently change the capability ranking.

review_notes.note: The rule that a sealed run is unusable when there is no way to state a correct answer is too absolute. Rubric-scored summaries, pairwise preference tasks and open-ended evaluations have no single correct answer but still have stable scoring rules.
review_notes.suggestion: Replace it with 'no stable scoring or comparison rule', and distinguish evaluation runs from exploratory generation.

review_notes.note: The operational advice is almost entirely pi-specific: the four CLI flags, MCP tool mounts, dust film tiles, `deepseek-4.1-flash` and the vault handbook. A reader using another agent product has to infer which channels to disable.
review_notes.suggestion: Keep dust as the running example but add a product-neutral checklist of channels to disable, and one short mapping for another runner.

review_notes.note: The canary tests only instruction leakage through a context file or skill. It does not test environment variables, home-directory credentials, network access, mounted tool paths, or a model echoing the prompt's schema example.
review_notes.suggestion: Make the seal check a small suite: canaries in several channels, a credential probe, a network probe, and an assertion that no answer key is reachable from any mount.

ratings.comment: The core shape and participants are clear, but the seal is overclaimed and the operational recipe is too pi-specific; I would use it after adding content-addressed specs and real container isolation.
